text:
Liam: Quick heads-up — running into a hang in the Go client when cancelling streaming requests. Context.Cancel() doesn't seem to free the HTTP/2 stream, and connections end up stuck in use. Anyone seen this?

Maya: Yep saw this before. Usually it's either the request not created with ctx or http2 transport not configured to close idle streams fast. Can you paste the client config?

Liam: Using our SDK default client (single global *http.Client). Transport is basically &http.Transport{MaxIdleConnsPerHost: 100, IdleConnTimeout: 90 * time.Second}. Request created with http.NewRequest (not NewRequestWithContext) — aha, that might be it. Repro steps:
1) Start a streaming generation (server sends tokens intermittently)
2) Cancel ctx after ~20s
3) Server stops, client goroutine stuck reading, connection shows active streams and doesn't return to pool

Nina: If request wasn't created with the ctx then cancellation won't interrupt RoundTrip. Use req = req.WithContext(ctx) or http.NewRequestWithContext. Also make sure you actually Close the response body on cancel.

Sam: Another angle: Go's net/http2 has had bugs where RST_STREAM isn't sent on client-side cancel unless the transport knows how to interrupt. If you reuse a long-lived Transport + http2.ConfigureTransport, ensure you don't set DisableKeepAlives = true accidentally. We also found making MaxIdleConnsPerHost > concurrent streams helps.

Olivia: For streaming we use streaming Reader loops that block on resp.Body.Read. If ctx cancels, the Read must return — that happens if req has ctx. Otherwise the goroutine sits there until server EOF. Also call resp.Body.Close() after cancel to force close.

Liam: OK switching to NewRequestWithContext and adding defer resp.Body.Close() in the stream goroutine. Any transport tuning suggestions for heavy multiplexed clients?

Maya: Tuning we use in prod for h2-heavy workloads: set Transport.IdleConnTimeout=30s, MaxIdleConnsPerHost=200, TLSHandshakeTimeout=5s, ExpectContinueTimeout=1s. Also set ForceAttemptHTTP2 = true to ensure h2 is used. If you use golang.org/x/net/http2, call http2.ConfigureTransport(&t) for more explicit control.

Sam: If you need aggressive eviction on cancel, decrease IdleConnTimeout and watch MaxConnsPerHost (Go1.19+). For HTTP/2 you might want to tweak http2.Transport: ReadIdleTimeout and PingTimeout if using http2's own transport.

Liam: Example I am trying now:
```go
tr := &http.Transport{
  MaxIdleConnsPerHost: 200,
  IdleConnTimeout: 30 * time.Second,
  ForceAttemptHTTP2: true,
}
http2.ConfigureTransport(tr) // from golang.org/x/net/http2
client := &http.Client{Transport: tr, Timeout: 0}
req := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "POST", url, body)
resp, err := client.Do(req)
// stream loop reads resp.Body, ctx cancel should break this and then we Close()
```

Nina: That looks reasonable. One more gotcha: if you wrap the response body in a bufio.Reader or similar, make sure the Close is still invoked. Also check for any io.Copy wrappers that ignore context.

Olivia: We also observed that when the server delays by >1m, the client can keep the stream open and server won't accept new streams on same connection. If you expect long idle servers, consider per-request timeouts + smaller MaxConcurrentStreams via server config.

Liam: Thanks folks — will run with these changes. If it repros I'll dump pprof/heap and netstat and paste here.

Sam: FYI I opened a small SDK PR to default our Go client to NewRequestWithContext + a small transport tweak: internal PR #2341. It adds a configurable IdleConnTimeout default 30s and docs note to Close bodies on cancel. Pinged @Maya for review.

Maya: Reviewing now, will comment inline. Also add a note to changelog about HTTP/2 streaming cancels. :+1:

Liam: Great — leaving my test run on over night and will report back tomorrow. Thanks!
